explanation: AKs is a premium hand that plays extremely well postflop due to its suit and high card strength. On the BTN vs an UTG open, 3-betting is standard for value. A smaller 3-bet size of around 3x the open is preferred because it keeps the SPR manageable, allows you to realize your positional advantage, and keeps in dominated hands like AQ, AJ, and KQ that might fold to a larger size.
villainRange: Tight ~14% open: 77+, ATs+, KTs+, QTs+, JTs, T9s, 98s, 87s, 76s, 65s, AQo+, KQo.

explanation: QQ is the third-best starting hand in poker. Against an MP open from the CO, 3-betting is mandatory for value. A standard 3-bet sizing of 3x the open is ideal. Flatting QQ in position is a mistake because it allows the blinds to come along cheaply and you lose the initiative. By 3-betting, you isolate the opener, build the pot with a strong hand, and define their range.
villainRange: ~17% open: 55+, A9s+, A5s-A4s, KTs+, QTs+, J9s+, T9s, 98s, 87s, 76s, 65s, AJo+, KQo.

explanation: Small to medium pocket pairs are excellent set-mining hands when the stacks are deep enough. With 100BB effective stacks, you have an implied odds ratio of 40:1 (risking 2.5BB to potentially win 100BB), which far exceeds the roughly 7.5:1 odds of flopping a set. Calling is preferred over 3-betting because 77 does not play well in 3-bet pots where the SPR is low and you face difficult decisions on overcards. Folding is too tight given the excellent implied odds.
villainRange: Tight ~14% open: 77+, ATs+, KTs+, QTs+, JTs, T9s, 98s, 87s, 76s, 65s, AQo+, KQo.

explanation: 89s is an ideal 3-bet bluff candidate on the BTN vs a CO open. It has excellent playability postflop with straight and flush potential, and blocks some of villain's continuing range. By 3-betting, you can win the pot preflop against folds, and when called, you have a hand that can flop strong draws and equity. This is a key part of a balanced 3-betting strategy where you mix value hands with suited connectors as bluffs.

A5s is one of the best 3-bet bluff hands from the BB against a BTN steal. It has an ace blocker reducing the chance villain has premium aces, it can make the nut flush, and the wheel straight potential gives it extra equity when called. The BTN opens a wide range (often 40-50% of hands), so they will fold frequently to a 3-bet. When called, you have enough equity to continue profitably on many flop textures.

KJs is a strong hand that plays well postflop but is not ideal as a 3-bet from the BB against a CO open. When you 3-bet, you often get called by hands that dominate you (AK, AJ, KQ) while folding out the weaker hands you dominate. By calling, you get an excellent price (needing only 31% equity to call), keep villain's range wide, and can leverage your hand's postflop playability with straight and flush draws. This is a textbook defend hand in the BB.

With pocket aces in the SB facing a 3-bet, 4-betting is mandatory. The sizing of around 2.5x the 3-bet is standard. Going all-in for 100BB would be a massive overbet that folds out everything except other premiums. A 4-bet to 22BB keeps in hands like QQ, JJ, AKs, and even some bluffs from aggressive opponents. You want to build the pot while keeping villain's range as wide as possible. If they 5-bet jam, you snap call.
villainRange: UTG open + BTN 3-bet. Linear 3-bet range: QQ+, AK, AQs, KQs, AJs. Mostly value — not many bluff combos vs a tight EP opener.

villainAction: LJ opens 2.5BB, HJ calls, CO calls
explanation: This is a textbook squeeze spot. JTs is an excellent candidate because it has strong postflop playability and the squeeze has high fold equity. When there are multiple callers in the pot, their ranges are capped (they would have 3-bet their strong hands). A squeeze to around 4x the open plus 1x per caller is standard sizing. You can win a 8.5BB pot uncontested frequently, and when called you have a connected suited hand that flops well.
villainRange: LJ open (~20%) + multiple cold-callers. Callers hold loose suited hands, pocket pairs, and suited broadways — capped, since QQ+/AK 3-bet.

explanation: At 35BB effective, pocket sixes are a clear open from the CO. Use a smaller sizing of 2.2BB which is standard in modern poker to risk less while still achieving the same goal. The hand has good equity against calling ranges and can flop a set for a big pot. Open-shoving 35BB is far too much with a hand that has decent postflop playability. Folding 66 from the CO would be extremely tight and a significant leak.
villainRange: No villain has entered yet — think about your opening range from this position and who is still left to act behind you.

explanation: K9s is not strong enough to continue facing an UTG open and a MP 3-bet. The 3-bettor's range here is extremely strong (typically QQ+, AK, sometimes JJ and AQs). Your hand is dominated by most of their value range and does not have enough playability to cold-call a 3-bet profitably out of position. Even though K9s is suited, the reverse implied odds are severe since when you make a King-high flush, they can have the Ace-high flush. This is a clear fold.
villainRange: UTG open + MP 3-bet. Linear 3-bet range: QQ+, AK, AQs, KQs, AJs. Mostly value — not many bluff combos vs a tight EP opener.

villainAction: Villain checks from BB (defended preflop vs your BTN open)
explanation: On Q72 rainbow, you have two overcards with backdoor straight draws. This is a great board to c-bet at a small sizing because the board heavily favors the preflop raiser's range (you have all the QQ, AA, KK, AQ combos). A 33% pot c-bet is ideal because it allows you to bet a very wide range profitably. Your AK has six outs to improve to top pair and applies pressure on villain's weak pairs and draws. The small sizing also keeps the pot manageable when you are behind.
villainRange: Flop calling range: top pair (weak-to-mid kicker), middle pair, pocket pairs below top card, gutshots, open-enders, flush draws. Capped — strong hands raise.

explanation: You have an open-ended straight draw (any 5 or T gives you a straight) on a board where you can credibly represent strong hands from the BB. Check-raising here is excellent because: (1) you have 8 outs to the nuts with two cards to come, giving you roughly 32% equity, (2) you can fold out hands like AK, AQ, AT that have you dominated on the current board, (3) when called, you still have strong draw equity, and (4) this balances your check-raising range with value hands like sets and two pair.
villainRange: Villain's c-bet range is close to their preflop open (60-75% of it). Contains top pair, overpairs, sets, and most draws/overcards/backdoors as bluffs. Range is polar on drier boards, more merged on wet boards.

villainAction: BB check-raises your c-bet from 5BB to 15BB
explanation: You flopped middle set on a coordinated KJ9 board. While the board is scary with straight possibilities (QT makes a straight), your set is too strong to fold. Calling is better than 3-betting because: (1) villain's check-raise range includes many draws and two-pair hands you crush, (2) 3-betting bloats the pot and only gets action from hands that beat you or have massive equity, and (3) by calling you keep villain's bluffs and semi-bluffs in their range. Plan to call safe turns and fold to completed straights/flushes if the action gets extreme.
villainRange: Polar check-raise range: sets, two pair, top pair strong kicker (value) + strong draws (open-enders, big flush draws, combo draws) as semi-bluffs. Balanced at 2:1 value:bluff on most textures.

explanation: You have the nut flush draw with an overcard on a board that favors your range as the preflop raiser. Betting 50% pot is optimal because: (1) you have 12+ outs (9 spade outs plus 3 aces for top pair), giving you roughly 47% equity against a pair, (2) this sizing applies maximum pressure on villain's marginal hands like 8x and underpairs, (3) you can continue barreling profitably on spade turns and ace turns, and (4) the larger sizing builds a pot for when you hit. Checking is too passive with this much equity and draw strength.
villainRange: Villain defended BB — wide and uncapped: suited connectors (T9s-54s), suited gappers, most suited aces, pocket pairs 22-JJ, broadway off-suits. Strong hands 3-bet, so this range has no premiums.

villainAction: BTN (3-bet caller) is waiting for your action
explanation: On an AK7 board after opening UTG and getting called by the BTN, your JJ is in a tough spot. Two overcards have hit the board. While you still beat some of villain's range (QQ, TT-22, suited connectors), you lose to a significant portion (AK, AQ, AJ, KQ, KJ). Checking is correct because: (1) c-betting gets called or raised only by hands that beat you, (2) villain's flatting range from the BTN contains many Ax and Kx hands, (3) checking allows you to pot control and potentially get to showdown cheaply, and (4) you can call a reasonable bet from villain if they stab.
villainRange: Villain flatted a 3-bet in position — capped: TT-JJ (mixed), AJs-AQs, KQs, AKo (mixed). No QQ+/AK hard-value (4-bet). Broadway + medium-pair.

explanation: You have a monster draw with a royal flush draw, an open-ended straight draw, and two overcards. Any heart (flush), any 9 or A (straight), plus K or Q outs give you approximately 21 outs with two cards to come, making you a significant favorite. Raising is correct because: (1) you have so much equity that you want to build the pot now, (2) you can fold out better made hands like weak two-pair or top pair, (3) if villain jams you can profitably call with your equity, and (4) this is far too strong a draw to just call and risk losing your fold equity.
villainRange: Donk-lead range: weak-to-medium made hands wanting protection (middle pair, bottom two, weak top pair) + the occasional trap (set/straight). Missing the nuts (would check-raise) and pure air (would check-fold).

villainAction: BB (3-bet pot, you 4-bet and they called) checks
explanation: In a 4-bet pot on a wet 876 two-tone board, you need to bet large with your overpair. This board is extremely coordinated with many straight and flush draws possible. A 75% pot bet is correct because: (1) you need to charge draws the maximum price since any 5, 9, T, or spade can be devastating, (2) villain's 4-bet calling range includes hands like JJ-99, AKs, AQs that can have straight draws or will pay off, (3) checking allows free cards that can destroy your equity, and (4) in 4-bet pots the SPR is already low so committing chips with AA is standard.
villainRange: Villain called a 4-bet — ultra-narrow: JJ-QQ, AQs, AJs (mixed), AKs/AKo. Range is tight, capped below KK, heavy on suited broadways.

explanation: You have a flush draw with a gutshot straight draw (any 2 gives you a wheel). With approximately 12 outs and two cards to come, you have around 45% equity against a typical c-bet range. Calling is preferred over raising because: (1) you have excellent implied odds at 94BB effective, (2) raising turns your hand into a semi-bluff that can get jammed on by strong Ax hands, (3) villain's large c-bet sizing indicates they may have a strong hand, and (4) you can realize your equity by seeing the turn cheaply and potentially getting paid off when you hit. Your position (closing the action in the BB) makes calling clean.
villainRange: Villain's c-bet range is close to their preflop open (60-75% of it). Contains top pair, overpairs, sets, and most draws/overcards/backdoors as bluffs. Range is polar on drier boards, more merged on wet boards.

villainAction: BB check-called flop, now checks turn
explanation: You have top pair top kicker on a relatively dry board after villain check-called the flop. The 7 turn is a brick that changes nothing. Betting 50% pot on the turn is ideal for value because: (1) you are ahead of villain's check-calling range which includes Ax with worse kickers, Jx, pocket pairs, and draws, (2) the sizing extracts value from second pair and weak top pair while not bloating the pot excessively, (3) you can comfortably bet again on safe rivers for a three-street value line, and (4) checking gives free cards to hands with 4-6 outs that should be paying to draw.
villainRange: Turn check range (flatted flop, checks turn): medium made hands planning to check-call, weak top pair, busted draws. Nuts rarely check — they protect this range with occasional slowplays.

villainAction: BB check-called flop, now checks turn
explanation: The King on the turn is a terrible card for your hand. On the flop of 862 you had a clear overpair to bet for value, but the K dramatically changes the situation. Checking is correct because: (1) the K is one of the worst turn cards as it hits villain's check-calling range hard (KQ, KJ, KT, K8, K6 all now beat you), (2) betting and getting raised puts you in a terrible spot, (3) by checking you pot control and can comfortably call a river bet or bet thin on safe rivers, and (4) villain's draws (straight draws, flush draws) have not improved so there is less urgency to bet for protection.
villainRange: Turn check range (flatted flop, checks turn): medium made hands planning to check-call, weak top pair, busted draws. Nuts rarely check — they protect this range with occasional slowplays.

villainAction: BB check-called flop bet, now checks again
explanation: The 2♥ turn gives you a flush draw in addition to your open-ended straight draw. You now have approximately 15 outs (8 straight outs + 9 flush outs minus 2 overlapping cards). Barreling the turn is correct because: (1) you have massive equity around 30-33% with one card to come, but the combined equity of fold equity + draw equity makes this a profitable bet, (2) you can fold out better made hands like weak top pair (T8, T7) and underpairs, (3) if called you still have a strong draw on the river, and (4) checking forfeits your fold equity with a hand that needs to improve to win at showdown.
villainRange: Turn check range (flatted flop, checks turn): medium made hands planning to check-call, weak top pair, busted draws. Nuts rarely check — they protect this range with occasional slowplays.

villainAction: BTN called flop c-bet, action on you
explanation: Despite holding pocket aces, the board is now KQJT with four to a straight. Any T in villain's range (AT, T9, T8) already has a straight. Many hands in BTN's calling range have hit this board hard: QJ, KJ, KQ for two pair, AT/T9 for straights, and any remaining spade draws. Checking is essential because: (1) you only beat a bluff or a very thin value hand, (2) betting into this board gets called or raised only by hands that crush you, (3) villain's flatting range connects heavily with broadway boards, and (4) you can potentially check-call a small bet or check-fold to a large bet, minimizing losses.
villainRange: Flop calling range: top pair (weak-to-mid kicker), middle pair, pocket pairs below top card, gutshots, open-enders, flush draws. Capped — strong hands raise.

explanation: The J on the turn pairs the board, which is actually a good card for your Kings. Your hand improves to Kings full if another K comes, and the paired board reduces the chance villain has trips (only one J remains). Betting 50% pot is correct because: (1) you have an overpair on a paired board which is a strong hand, (2) villain's check-calling range on the flop includes many Jx, pocket pairs (88-TT), and draws that will pay off, (3) if villain has a J they now have trips and will likely check-raise giving you clear information, and (4) you build the pot for a comfortable river shove.
villainRange: Turn check range (flatted flop, checks turn): medium made hands planning to check-call, weak top pair, busted draws. Nuts rarely check — they protect this range with occasional slowplays.

explanation: You have an open-ended straight draw (any 5 or T completes your straight) and the A on the turn is an excellent barrel card. Betting is correct because: (1) the Ace is a great scare card that represents AK, AQ, AJ which are all in your preflop opening range, (2) villain's flop check-call range is mostly 7x, 6x, pocket pairs like 88-TT, and small flush draws that all hate the Ace, (3) you still have 8 outs to the nuts if called, and (4) this is a key concept in poker known as a 'double barrel bluff' using a favorable turn card to represent a strong range.
villainRange: Turn check range (flatted flop, checks turn): medium made hands planning to check-call, weak top pair, busted draws. Nuts rarely check — they protect this range with occasional slowplays.

villainAction: CO bet flop, you called. CO now bets 14BB (50%)
explanation: You have top pair with a good kicker. The T pairing on the turn is concerning because villain could have TT for a full house or AT for a better two pair. However, calling is correct because: (1) your hand beats a significant portion of villain's value range (AK, AQ are the only Ax hands that beat you, and AT specifically), (2) folding top pair strong kicker to a single turn barrel is too tight, (3) you have position to control the river action, and (4) villain could be barreling with worse aces or missed spade draws. Raising turns your hand into a bluff since better hands call and worse hands fold.
villainRange: Turn betting range: value (top pair+ kicker, overpairs, sets, two pair) + draws that picked up equity. Polar on drawy turns, merged on brick turns.

villainAction: BB check-called flop and turn, now checks river
explanation: You have top pair top kicker on a bricked out board. Villain has check-called two streets, indicating a medium-strength hand like Ax with a weaker kicker (AQ, AJ, AT), 99, or possibly a slow-played set. Betting 50% pot is optimal because: (1) you are clearly ahead of villain's check-calling range and need to extract value, (2) this sizing gets called by all worse Ax hands and pocket pairs, (3) going all-in is too large and folds out the hands you want to call, (4) checking is a massive mistake that forfeits value from a hand that beats 80%+ of villain's range.
villainRange: Capped river check range: showdown hands (2nd/3rd pair, ace-high), busted draws, and give-up bluffs. Strong value rarely checks the river — it protects with a small slowplay frequency.

villainAction: CO bet flop, checked turn, now bets 30BB (75%) on river
explanation: This is a classic bluff-catching spot where folding is correct. The line of bet-check-bet is very polarized on this runout. Villain's river bet of 75% pot on the K river tells a clear story: they either have a strong hand (Kx that improved, JJ, KK, sets, two pair) or a missed draw bluffing. However, the K is one of the worst river cards for your TT because: (1) many hands that checked the turn for pot control now have top pair (KQ, KT, K9), (2) villain's flop c-bet range includes many Kx hands, (3) the price you're getting (need 28.6% equity) is not met against this polarized range, and (4) you block very few bluffs in villain's range.
villainRange: Merged river bet range: thin value (weak top pair, overpairs, some pairs needing protection) + a smaller share of bluffs. Smaller sizing = thinner value-heavy range.

villainAction: BB check-called flop and turn, now checks river
explanation: Your QJ missed completely -- you have Queen high with a busted straight draw. However, this is an excellent bluffing spot on the river. Betting 50% pot is correct because: (1) villain's line of check-call, check-call, check shows a capped medium-strength range (pairs like T9, 87, 98, pocket pairs 55-77), (2) your QJ blocks some of villain's stronger calling hands (QT, JT), (3) at 50% pot sizing you need villain to fold only 33% of the time to break even, (4) representing an overpair or a strong hand that barreled all three streets is very credible from the CO, and (5) checking guarantees you lose since you cannot win at showdown.
villainRange: Capped river check range: showdown hands (2nd/3rd pair, ace-high), busted draws, and give-up bluffs. Strong value rarely checks the river — it protects with a small slowplay frequency.

villainAction: BB check-called flop and turn, now leads 35BB on river
explanation: You have a set of eights but this board is more dangerous than it first looks. The wheel straight (any 3-4 makes A-2-3-4-5) is the actual nuts and sits squarely in BB's check-call range. Trip aces (any AA, AQ, A5, A2 with an A on river giving two pair) and trip queens (QQ) also beat you. Villain's surprise lead after check-calling twice is a meaningful polarization signal — they often have a hand they want to value bet, not bluff. Calling is correct because: (1) you still beat the weaker portion of the value range (Ax two pair) and pick off a thin bluff range, (2) jamming only gets called by the hands that beat you (wheel, set+, trip A) and folds out worse, (3) at 48BB behind into an 87BB pot you have a clean call price without committing more on a board where you are not the nuts.
villainRange: Capped river check range: showdown hands (2nd/3rd pair, ace-high), busted draws, and give-up bluffs. Strong value rarely checks the river — it protects with a small slowplay frequency.

villainAction: BTN calls flop bet, calls turn bet, river action on you
explanation: After betting flop and turn with pocket nines on a K743J board, checking the river is correct. This is a common spot where players over-bet for value but their hand is not strong enough. The reasons to check are: (1) villain called two streets on a board with a King and a Jack, meaning their range is heavily weighted toward Kx and Jx hands that all beat you, (2) very few worse hands call a third bet (maybe 88, TT but these often fold earlier), (3) any bet gets called only by better hands and folds out worse hands, which is the definition of a bad value bet, (4) checking allows you to win at showdown against missed draws and give up the minimum against better hands.
villainRange: Merged river bet range: thin value (weak top pair, overpairs, some pairs needing protection) + a smaller share of bluffs. Smaller sizing = thinner value-heavy range.

villainAction: BB check-called flop, checked turn (you checked back), now checks river
explanation: You rivered the nut flush with A9 of spades. The board ran out K732J with four spades. Betting 75% pot is the correct sizing because: (1) your hand is extremely strong (nut flush) and you need to maximize value, (2) villain's range after check-calling the flop includes many Kx, 7x, and any hand with a single spade that now has a one-card flush, (3) villain may have a smaller flush (any single spade in hand) and will find it very difficult to fold, (4) the 75% sizing looks like a potential bluff to villain which induces calls, and (5) smaller sizings leave too much value on the table with a hand this strong.
villainRange: Capped river check range: showdown hands (2nd/3rd pair, ace-high), busted draws, and give-up bluffs. Strong value rarely checks the river — it protects with a small slowplay frequency.

villainAction: BB defended, you bet flop, bet turn. BB calls both. River action on you
explanation: You have a complete airball with six high and a busted flush draw. However, this is one of the best river bluff spots because: (1) the board is KQ8-4-T and you have barreled two streets representing a strong range, (2) the T river completes AJ for a straight, which you can credibly represent, (3) by shoving all-in for a pot-sized bet, villain needs to call off their stack with one pair which is psychologically very difficult, (4) villain's double-call range is mostly Kx and Qx that will face enormous pressure from an all-in, (5) your hand has zero showdown value so checking guarantees a loss, and (6) the overbet sizing makes this a very profitable bluff if villain folds more than 50% of the time.
villainRange: Merged river bet range: thin value (weak top pair, overpairs, some pairs needing protection) + a smaller share of bluffs. Smaller sizing = thinner value-heavy range.

explanation: With pocket Aces in early position, you should always open raise. A standard 2.5BB open is preferred in modern poker to keep your range balanced and to avoid bloating the pot in a way that narrows your perceived range. Limping Aces is a common beginner mistake that allows multiple opponents to see a cheap flop, reducing your equity significantly.
villainRange: No villain has entered yet — think about your opening range from this position and who is still left to act behind you.

explanation: Suited connectors like 76s play very well from the cutoff position. You have only two players left to act (BTN and blinds), giving you good fold equity. When called, your hand has excellent playability postflop with straight and flush draw potential. Always raise rather than limp to maintain the initiative.
villainRange: No villain has entered yet — think about your opening range from this position and who is still left to act behind you.

explanation: Small pocket pairs like 55 are classic set-mining hands. You are getting excellent implied odds with 100BB effective stacks, as you will win a large pot roughly 1 in 8 times when you flop a set. 3-betting is too aggressive with this hand against an UTG range, and folding is too tight given the implied odds. Calling and playing for set value is the optimal line.
villainRange: Tight ~14% open: 77+, ATs+, KTs+, QTs+, JTs, T9s, 98s, 87s, 76s, 65s, AQo+, KQo.

explanation: In the big blind facing a button open, Q9 suited is a profitable defend. The button opens a very wide range, and you are getting 3.5:1 on a call after posting your blind. Your hand has decent suited high-card equity and can make strong flushes and straights. 3-betting is viable occasionally as a bluff, but calling is the standard and most profitable play.

AKo in the small blind facing an open and a cold call is a textbook squeeze spot. You should size up your 3-bet to around 14BB because there are two opponents who have shown interest in the pot. A larger sizing punishes the cold caller who often has a capped, medium-strength range. AK has too much equity to just flat call out of position in a multiway pot.
villainRange: CO open (~27%) + BTN flat — loose suited hands, pocket pairs, suited broadways. Capped because strong hands 3-bet.

explanation: Kings are the second-best starting hand and should almost always be 4-bet for value when facing a 3-bet. A sizing of around 20BB keeps your 4-bet range balanced and gives your opponent room to make mistakes by calling or 5-bet shoving with worse hands. Going all-in preflop is too aggressive at 100BB deep and folds out most of villain's bluffs.
villainRange: BTN 3-bet. Polar 3-bet range: QQ+, AK for value; A5s-A2s, K9s-K7s, Q9s-Q8s, 76s, 65s as bluffs. Strong hands + suited playability bluffs.

explanation: JTs is one of the best suited connectors and plays beautifully on the button. While 3-betting is a viable option, flatting in position allows you to realize your excellent equity postflop. You can flop straights, flushes, two pairs, and strong draws. Being in position means you control the pot size and can extract value or bluff efficiently on later streets.
villainRange: ~17% open: 55+, A9s+, A5s-A4s, KTs+, QTs+, J9s+, T9s, 98s, 87s, 76s, 65s, AJo+, KQo.

explanation: A4 suited is an excellent 3-bet bluff candidate from the cutoff. It has a blocker to strong Ace-x hands (reducing the chance villain has AA, AK, AQ), and when called, it retains equity through its flush draw and backdoor straight potential. This hand performs better as a 3-bet than a flat call because it is difficult to play profitably out of position postflop with a weak kicker.

With a short stack of 25BB, pocket eights are a strong squeeze-shove candidate from the big blind. You have significant fold equity against the opener and the cold caller, and when called, 88 has solid equity against most calling ranges. Flatting out of position multiway with a short stack is problematic because you cannot effectively set mine with only 25BB.
villainRange: CO open (~27%) + BTN flat — loose suited hands, pocket pairs, suited broadways. Capped because strong hands 3-bet.

explanation: KQo on the button facing an UTG open and a cold call is a spot where flatting is preferred. While KQ is a strong hand, 3-betting runs into the UTG player's strong range and risks getting 4-bet off your equity. By calling in position, you keep the pot smaller and play postflop with a positional advantage. Your hand has good equity realization in position against both opponents.
villainRange: UTG open (~14%) + MP flat — loose suited hands, pocket pairs, suited broadways. Capped because strong hands 3-bet.

explanation: Queens are the third-best starting hand and should always be opened with a raise. A standard 2.5BB raise is the modern standard from middle position, keeping your opening size consistent with the rest of your range. This prevents observant opponents from exploiting different sizings. You want action from worse hands while not overcommitting preflop.
villainRange: No villain has entered yet — think about your opening range from this position and who is still left to act behind you.

explanation: 98 suited is a strong enough hand to open from the hijack position. It has excellent playability postflop with straight and flush potential, making it a profitable open in a position where only four players remain. Limping is never correct with this hand as it forfeits the initiative and invites the blinds to see a cheap flop. Opening maintains fold equity and board coverage.
villainRange: No villain has entered yet — think about your opening range from this position and who is still left to act behind you.

explanation: Tens are a strong hand but face a difficult spot when 3-bet. Against a cutoff 3-bet range, TT has good equity but does not benefit much from 4-betting because it folds out worse hands and gets called only by better ones. Calling keeps villain's bluffs in their range and allows you to play postflop. Your hand is strong enough to continue but not strong enough to build a large pot preflop.
villainRange: CO 3-bet. Polar 3-bet range: QQ+, AK for value; A5s-A2s, K9s-K7s, Q9s-Q8s, 76s, 65s as bluffs. Strong hands + suited playability bluffs.

explanation: KJs is a strong defending hand from the big blind against a cutoff open. You are closing the action and getting a good price. explanation: Even with QQ, a sub-30BB stack in the big blind faces a brutal ICM reality here. The CO jammer's range at that sizing is narrow (TT+, AK, some AQs), giving QQ about 52% equity when called. But ICM pressure converts that raw 52% equity into a negative EV call near the bubble because busting costs you the pay jump while eliminating the jammer doubles you up. QQ calls in chip-EV but folds in ICM-EV — one of the classic bubble adjustments separating cash players from tournament pros.
villainRange: Nash ~20BB jam: 77+, ATs+, KJs+, QJs, AJo+, KQo. Blockers + equity vs calling range.

This is a Nash re-shove region learned from push-fold charts: hands like KQs are at the top of your re-jam range because they combine equity against calling ranges with blocker value to the top of villain's range.
villainRange: ~40% open/complete: 22+, A2s+, K5s+, Q8s+, J8s+, T8s+, 97s+, 86s+, 75s+, 65s, 54s, A8o+, KTo+, QTo+, JTo.

KQs in the BB facing a BTN open and SB flat is a premium squeeze. The SB cold-call is very capped — it rarely contains AA or KK, which would 3-bet, so their range is heavy on pocket pairs 22-99 and middling suited broadways. KQs dominates large swaths of that calling range and has excellent equity when called. Flatting is inferior because you invite the BTN to squeeze you and give up positional EV postflop.
villainRange: BTN open (~47%) + SB cold-flat. Capped SB flat range: 22-JJ, ATs-AQs, KJs-KQs, QJs, JTs, T9s, 98s, ATo-AQo, KJo-KQo, QJo. QQ+ and most AK 3-bet, so the top of this range is missing.

explanation: Small pocket pairs 22 thrive at deep stacks. At 100BB effective you have implied-odds ratios exceeding the 7.5:1 set-flop odds many times over. Calling is better than 3-betting because 22 plays poorly in 3-bet pots with SPR ~4 where you are often capped by overcards. Set-mining passively from IP or the blinds preserves the exact scenario in which 22 is most profitable: hit a set 1-in-8 and stack an overpair or top-pair hand.

explanation: QQ facing a 4-bet at 75BB is a call in position, not a 5-bet jam. Against a typical 4-bet value range (JJ+, AK) you have 40-45% equity which is fine to play postflop but disaster to get it in. Calling preserves implied odds when you flop a set, realizes equity on brick boards where you get to check down, and folds cleanly when overcards arrive and villain barrels large. Jamming is -EV because you fold out the dominated combos and get called only by AA/KK/AK.
villainRange: Polar 4-bet: QQ+, AK for value; A5s-A4s, sometimes KQs as bluffs. Blocker-heavy bluff selection.

explanation: Isolating the limper with AJs from late position is exactly the spot this hand wants. You inherit the initiative, reduce the field to go heads-up with a playable hand, and take the pot down uncontested a meaningful percentage of the time. Sizing 4-5x over a limper is the standard exploitation — a flat 3x doesn't punish the limp enough and tends to invite the blinds into a multiway pot where your equity realization plummets.
villainRange: Loose-passive limp range: 22-TT, Axs, suited broadways that don't 3-bet, suited gappers, occasional KQ/AJ limp-trap. Uncapped but rarely the nuts — often the second-nuts.

explanation: In a 3-bet pot out of position on a low board with a pair on it, range-betting small is the modern solver approach. Your overpair AA is comfortably ahead of villain's preflop flatting range; more importantly, the texture denies villain almost no equity, so you can bet your entire range (value, bluffs, and everything in between) at 25% pot. This sizing turns every hand into a small-value extractor while denying free cards to over-pairs that aren't in villain's range.
villainRange: Villain flatted a 3-bet in position — capped: TT-JJ (mixed), AJs-AQs, KQs, AKo (mixed). No QQ+/AK hard-value (4-bet). Broadway + medium-pair.

The raise also starts to look balanced with your check-raise bluff combos (QJ, JT with backdoors), so villain cannot simply fold top pair, worse two pair, and sets.

villainAction: Hero opened, CO and BB called (3-way)
explanation: In a multiway pot (3+ players) c-betting frequencies drop dramatically because each additional opponent reduces your fold equity and adds someone holding a piece of the board. AK on a low disconnected flop multiway is a textbook give-up: you have two overcards but no backdoors, cannot rep the board, and any call behind kills your equity realization. Check-folding is far superior to c-betting into multiple opponents.
villainRange: Multiway callers' ranges skew to pocket pairs (set-mining), suited connectors (implied odds), and suited aces. Strong made hands are rare — cold-calling multiway prefers big-implied hands.

Betting turns your hand face up — villain folds worse and calls / raises better. Checking realizes your equity cheaply, keeps villain's bluffs in the pot for the turn and river, and lets you showdown enough hands to break even. This is solver-approved because it protects the rest of your IP checking range, including slow-plays and strong showdown hands.

Polar overbetting is mandatory: it gets max value from kings, two pair, sevens, and trips while being balanced by bluffs that share the same sizing. A smaller sizing extracts far less against a range that is sticky to any bet size.
villainRange: Capped river check range: showdown hands (2nd/3rd pair, ace-high), busted draws, and give-up bluffs. Strong value rarely checks the river — it protects with a small slowplay frequency.

explanation: Top pair top kicker is a strong hand but not when you're capped and villain donks a huge river. Their range for this line (call-call-lead jam) is overwhelmingly weighted to rivered straights (97, J9, 79) and sets that got there. AQ beats only bluffs, and BB's bluff frequency is far too low here. Folding is disciplined; calling is a classic leak for players who overvalue top pair in polarized river spots.
villainRange: Polar river jam: straights, flushes, full houses, sets + balanced bluff combos with blockers. Very little medium-strength value — expect either the nuts or nothing.

explanation: River probe after villain checked back the turn: jack-ten rivered two pair on a runout that is miles ahead of any hand that chose to check back. A 40% pot sizing is the sweet spot — it extracts value from king-x, jack-x, and the occasional ten-x while keeping your bluffing frequency balanced on the same sizing. Probing small is better than going big because the turn check-back capped villain's range and big bets fold out too much of the weak portion you beat.
villainRange: IP check-back range (capped): marginal showdown hands — middle pair, ace-high with showdown, weak top pair, busted turn draws. Strong value bets; pure air bluffs; this range is what's left.

explanation: Quads on a board where villain just bet the river is the ultimate check-raise spot. Villain's betting range is polarized between full houses, trips with good kickers, and bluffs — all of them pay off a raise more often than you might expect because villain cannot credibly rep quads themselves. Jamming all-in is strictly better than a small raise: it maximizes the value you extract from full houses and still gets called by sticky trips + paid bluffs that convince themselves you're capped.
villainRange: Merged river bet range: thin value (weak top pair, overpairs, some pairs needing protection) + a smaller share of bluffs. Smaller sizing = thinner value-heavy range.

It sets a cheap price for villain's bluff-catchers, denies villain the ability to check back weak showdown, and induces raise-bluffs from polarized villains who interpret small bets as weakness. Big betting is fine but loses EV against the chunk of villain's range that would value-bet thinly if checked.

Big betting is fine but loses EV against the chunk of villain's range that would value-bet thinly if checked.
villainRange: IP check-back range (capped): marginal showdown hands — middle pair, ace-high with showdown, weak top pair, busted turn draws. Strong value bets; pure air bluffs; this range is what's left.
